_note: Harlow Bridge's townsfolk on Market Square and Meetinghouse Hill (decision 0476): fourteen people, Matt's approved lines word for word. Each says their 'now' lines until the tower clock strikes (harlow_stone_woke), then their 'after' line. Dr. Wolcott, Mrs. Ames and the Goodell children have a second talk about Thadeous before the clock strikes. Voices and facts are in docs/regions/harlow-bridge.md.

lines.text: Wool's up. Lamp oil's up. Everything's up but the mill.
I measure it twice. You'd be surprised what a yard does in the cold.
Wheels going. The hands'll want cloth by Saturday. I've measured it already.
I've a powder for the frost. Camphor and chalk, mostly. It doesn't work, but people like to be doing something.
Half the town's on my wintergreen. The other half's at the Tankard.
Nobody's bought the powder since the clock struck. I'm taking it as a compliment to the powder.
He looks at your boots before he looks at you.
Road clay. Hill clay over it. And something white in the welts.
You've been up past the wall. Nobody goes up past the wall.
Same white in the welts. Less of it now.
I set every notice on that board. Half of them twice, because people change their minds.
If you want something done in this town, put it on the board. If you want it done right, ask me who wrote it.
I set one this morning. "Mill running. Hands wanted at noon." Nobody's needed that one in a month.
There's an ordinance against singing in the square after ten. I wrote it for one man. He has never once been home by ten.
I don't rule on the weather. People keep asking me to.
The clock struck at half past two in the morning. Under the ordinance that's disturbing the peace. I'm letting it go.
Chilblains. Every hand on Mill Street. Standing about in the cold doesn't agree with men who aren't used to standing about.
You'll want to know what I think of the frost. I think it's cold.
He comes to me about his throat every winter. It's never his throat.
Two hands back on the wheel this morning with their fingers wrapped. I told them not to. Nobody listens to a doctor when there's work.
Stage still stops here. Stage always stops here. That's why there's a Harlow Bridge.
Horses don't like the north road this year. They'll go up the Pasture Lane as far as the bars and no further.
Took the gray up the lane this morning. Went right past the bars. Didn't even look round.
Laid over till Thursday. The road down's clear. The road up I won't drive after dark, and I've driven it twenty years.
I carry the news both ways. Harlow's news this month is that it's cold.
Every inn on the road will want to hear about that clock. I'll tell it slower each time.
I sit at this window. Somebody has to.
If you're looking for anybody, ask me. I'll know where they went, and most of the time why.
He goes up the lane every night about nine. Comes down about four. I don't sleep much either.
He didn't come down at four last night. I watched till it was light. Then he came down singing, and I went to bed.
You're the fox.
He can't be the fox. He's a stranger.
Strangers can be foxes.
We're not allowed to sing the Burnbottom song. Mother says.
It goes...
Eli.
The clock went in the night. I counted to three and then I fell asleep.
It went to three. I counted all of it.
I don't hold with the Tankard. I don't hold with singing on a weekday, and I don't hold with that man.
I walked him home Tuesday. He sang the whole way. I don't hold with that either.
The clock struck in the night. I went down to the meetinghouse in case it was a fire. It wasn't. I stayed a while anyway.
School's shut till the cold breaks. Penhallow's orders. The stove can't keep up and neither can I.
The singing school filled the meetinghouse every winter when I was a girl. The Reverend wants it back. So do I, and I'm not too proud to say so.
Clock's going. If the school can open, the singing school can. Somebody tell the Reverend I said so.
His dinner. Every noon I carry it up, and every noon the last one's still there.
He puts his hand on the works and stands there. Forty years married, and I'd never seen him stand still.
He ate his dinner. Both of them. Then he wound her, and came home, and slept.
Mr. Penhallow's in the mill office. Mr. Penhallow's always in the mill office.
His father raised the dam. You'll hear people say it was the right thing. You won't hear it from me, and you didn't hear that from me either.
He stood at the window the whole night the clock struck. I brought him tea at three. He said thank you. He has never once said thank you.
